edits.old: None. The contract publishes the task-queue and activity-contract convention rather than a workflow: a service's worker polls only its own task queue `rwb-<short>` in namespace `rwb-recovery`, publishes its typed activity interfaces in a contract jar, and calls another service only through that interface or a child workflow on the owner's queue (Architecture v5 slides 23 and 24; Architecture v5 slide 11). The platform task queue is task queue `rwb-platform`; the document records it as the platform queue and owns no workflow on it in this story.
edits.new: None. The contract publishes the task-queue and activity-contract convention rather than a workflow: a service's worker polls only its own task queue `rwb-<short>` in namespace `rwb-recovery`, publishes its typed activity interfaces in a contract jar, and calls another service only through that interface or a child workflow on the owner's queue (Architecture v5 slides 23 and 24; Architecture v5 slide 11). Each service registers one worker on its own queue under its own workload identity and a client certificate whose subject names the service; the platform creates the queues at install from the service catalogue and refuses a worker that polls another queue; each service has its own codec key under the namespace key; the smoke workflow starts through RWB-PLT-E1070-APP on one named service queue. The platform task queue is task queue `rwb-platform`, the platform team's queue outside the 19 service queues (RWB-PLT-WF); the document records it as the platform queue and owns no workflow on it in this story.
